book.title: The Telegraph All New Toughie Crossword, book 1

clue.text: "L_ Type of housing that can be closed in two seconds

indicators.note: 'in' places the word for closed inside the pair of words for seconds

blocks.note: scanning debris printed before the clue, with no part in it
to second a proposal is to back it, so two seconds are two backs
a door pushed to is closed

explanation.surface: An estate agent touts a style of house that can be shut up in moments.
explanation.walkthrough: The page's stray '"L_' before the clue is scanning debris and plays no part. BACK-TO-BACK houses share their rear wall with the row behind, typical of old northern English terraces.
explanation.definitionFit: Back-to-back is a recognised style of terraced dwelling, where two rows of houses share a common rear wall.

clue.text: Make white cable newly connected to hot

indicators.note: 'newly' suggests the word is made over afresh, in a new letter order

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: An electrician wires a new white cable to the live terminal.
explanation.definitionFit: To bleach something is to remove its colour, turning it white.

clue.text: Texan biscuit business approved even bits of rice

indicators.note: the even bits are the letters in the second and fourth places

blocks.note: Co. is short for company, a business
OK means approved
second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A Texas firm signs off on a cracker made with rice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Texan' marks the American word: what Britons call a biscuit, Americans call a cookie.
explanation.definitionFit: Cookie is the standard American term for a sweet biscuit, so a Texan would use it.

clue.text: Small beer? Excitedly slurp it after university game indoors

indicators.note: doing something excitedly is doing it in a wild, disordered way
'after' sends the words before it second, behind the university letter

blocks.note: small beer means unimportant matters, trivia
U is the abbreviation for university
taken as written

explanation.surface: Students noisily gulp weak ale after a match.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters supply the L that ends TRIVIAL as well as PURSUIT. Small beer is weak ale, or by extension anything unimportant.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivial Pursuit is a general-knowledge board game, played round a table indoors.

clue.text: Yeoman producing crab apple?

blocks.note: to crab and to beef both mean to grumble
an eating apple is called an eater

explanation.surface: A farmer's land grows a sour wild apple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crab apple' reads as one fruit, but splits into a complaint and a dessert apple. Yeoman Warders at the Tower of London are nicknamed Beefeaters.
explanation.definitionFit: Beefeater is the popular name for a Yeoman Warder of the Tower of London, or the Yeoman of the Guard.

clue.text: Teacher, in officer's company, served up snack

indicators.note: being in someone's company here means sitting within that word
in a down clue, served up means written bottom to top

blocks.note: PC, a police constable, is the officer whose company the teacher keeps
pupils address a male teacher as sir

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher dining with officers in the mess is handed a nibble.
explanation.walkthrough: A crisp is what Americans call a potato chip.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisp is a thin fried slice of potato sold in bags as a snack.

clue.text: Gemstone belonging to bishops (no record is about)

indicators.note: 'no' says the following items are absent from the longer word, so they are struck out

blocks.note: episcopal means relating to bishops
an EP is an extended-play record
taken as written
c, for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A jewel in a bishop's ring is described, with a parenthetical aside about missing records.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike EP, IS and C from EPISCOPAL and OPAL is what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is a precious stone prized for its shifting play of colours.

clue.text: Parking negligent around back of the building

indicators.note: 'around' wraps one word about the letter that follows
the back of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
remiss means careless of duty
last letter

explanation.surface: Careless parking at the rear of the block.
explanation.definitionFit: Premises are a building with its grounds, as in 'no smoking on the premises'.

clue.text: Monthly tours included "2nd of August — Devon resort"

indicators.note: the 2nd of a word is the letter in its second place
something that tours travels round, so the letters move about

blocks.note: taken as written
second letter

explanation.surface: A holiday programme lists August 2nd at a seaside town in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: Devon is a county in south-west England; Lynmouth is a small harbour village on its north coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Lynmouth is a seaside village and holiday spot on the north coast of the English county of Devon.

clue.text: Exhausted comic nose for fun exploit that's broadcast

indicators.note: something comic is absurd and topsy-turvy, so the letters are jumbled
broadcast words are heard rather than read, so the sound counts

blocks.note: taken letter for letter
an exploit is a feat, which is heard the same as the plural of foot

explanation.surface: A worn-out comedian televises a stunt with a red nose for charity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comic nose' suggests Comic Relief's red noses, but comic only jumbles the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Being run off one's feet is an idiom for being so busy that one is worn out.

clue.text: From April, ocean's reviewed for source of food poisoning

indicators.note: 'From' says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows
to review is to look back over, so the run is read backwards

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of April and the start of ocean

explanation.surface: A spring report on the sea traces the cause of an outbreak of food poisoning.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of ocean's is part of the surface only; the run ends inside ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: E. coli is a gut bacterium whose harmful strains are a notorious cause of food poisoning.

clue.text: 11__ Timeless image preserved by repaint periodically, and refined

indicators.note: 'periodically' means at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept
'Timeless' means without time, so its abbreviation T is dropped
something preserved by another is kept safe inside it

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
a picture is an image

explanation.surface: Restoring an old picture by repainting it here and there leaves it looking elegant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'image preserved by repaint' tempts one to look for a word hidden in repaint; instead the shortened image is wrapped in the letters repaint yields.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicurean has cultivated, discriminating taste, especially in food and wine, so is refined.

clue.text: Food provides juiciness when pulped, removing outside

indicators.note: removing the outside strips the first and last letters from the word
pulped fruit is crushed out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: juiciness without its outer J and S

explanation.surface: Mashed fruit, peeled first, gives a dish its succulence.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuisine is a style of cooking, and by extension the food produced, as in 'the hotel's cuisine'.

clue.text: Hard to avoid loaf of bread in ace condition

indicators.note: to avoid something is to leave it out, so that letter is dropped
'in' puts the shortened brand name inside the word for ace

blocks.note: Hovis is a well-known British brand of bread loaf
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
an ace is an expert, a pro

explanation.surface: Keeping a loaf in perfect shape is tricky.
explanation.walkthrough: Hovis is a long-established British brand of brown bread; without its H it goes inside PRO, after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: A proviso is a stipulation attached to an agreement, a condition that must be met.

clue.text: OAPteams left shuffling feet around London

indicators.note: shuffling moves things about into a new order, here the letters

blocks.note: taken letter for letter; the scan has run 'OAP teams' together

explanation.surface: Pensioners' sides leave the field dragging their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feet around London' signals Cockney rhyming slang, where plates of meat rhymes with feet. OAP is an old-age pensioner.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang, spoken in London's East End, plates of meat stands for feet.

clue.text: Laurel encircles American (on annual return), no. 1 charity worker

indicators.note: to encircle something is to surround it, so the rest goes inside

blocks.note: Am. is the abbreviation for American
AR is the abbreviation for a company's annual return
I is the Roman numeral for one
Stan Laurel, of the comedy pair Laurel and Hardy

explanation.surface: A laurel wreath is presented to an American, the top fundraiser, at the year's accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laurel' looks like a garland, but it is the comedian. The Samaritans are a UK charity offering a listening line to people in distress.
explanation.definitionFit: A Samaritan is a volunteer for the Samaritans helpline, and more widely anyone who helps strangers.

clue.text: Foreign chap, following streetmap, enters to try Spanish course

indicators.note: a foreign version of the word is a strange rearrangement of it
'following' puts the jumbled word after the map
the pair enters, going inside the word for try

blocks.note: the A-Z is the classic British street atlas
taken as written
to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: A foreign tourist, map in hand, walks into a restaurant to sample a Spanish dish.
explanation.walkthrough: An A-Z is a book of street maps, best known for London.
explanation.definitionFit: Gazpacho is a chilled tomato soup from Andalusia, served as a course of a Spanish meal.

clue.text: Lent requires cider to be emptied, abandoned

indicators.note: the word for lent needs the next piece taken inside it
emptying a word removes its contents, leaving only its outer letters

blocks.note: to sub someone is to lend them money as an advance
first and last letters

explanation.surface: During Lent, the drink is poured away and given up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lent' looks like the fast before Easter; its capital letter is only its place in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that is scrubbed has been cancelled or dropped, so abandoned.

clue.text: Bill gathers another metre, making dress

indicators.note: another version of the word is a different arrangement of its letters
to gather something in is to hold it inside

blocks.note: a bill is an account
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tailor's bill swells because the dress needed an extra metre of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: An accoutrement is an item of dress or equipment, especially an accessory worn with clothing.

clue.text: Fleet Street promoted by constant fliers

indicators.note: in a down clue, promoted means moved upward, read bottom to top

blocks.note: c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light
the Royal Air Force, the national fleet of aircraft
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Fleet Street, London's old newspaper district, is lifted by constant leaflets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet Street' reads as one place, but splits into two words with separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Craft is a word for aircraft, so crafts are machines that fly.

clue.text: Alcoholic drink for each academic returning

indicators.note: something returning heads back the way it came, so it is read backwards

blocks.note: per means for each
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A spirit is poured for every lecturer coming back.
explanation.definitionFit: Pernod is a French brand of aniseed-flavoured spirit, a strong aperitif.

clue.text: Chicken soup's stirred wrong

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
a sin is a wrong

explanation.surface: Someone has made a mess of the chicken soup.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'has': soup has, stirred, then wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A poussin is a very young chicken raised for the table.

clue.text: Imbecile television beginning to nark over time

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter
set over the time letter, it takes that letter's place

blocks.note: telly is informal British for television
first letter
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Mindless television starts to irritate after a while.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the T of TELLY for N. Nelly, as in 'not on your nelly', is old British slang for a silly person.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelly is dated British slang for a foolish or weak person, a nitwit.

clue.text: Book about tennis stroke

blocks.note: re means about, concerning
the stroke that starts each tennis point

explanation.surface: A title on the subject of a tennis shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a noun here, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To book a table or seat is to reserve it in advance.

clue.text: Telegraph snaps England footballer heading for trendy convertible

indicators.note: to snap something up is to grab it and hold it inside
the heading of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a cable is a telegram, sent by telegraph
Rio Ferdinand, long-serving England centre-back
first letter

explanation.surface: A newspaper photographs an England star driving a fashionable soft-top.
explanation.walkthrough: The Telegraph is also the newspaper this puzzle ran in; here it is a telegram.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabriolet is a car with a folding roof, the classic convertible.

clue.text: Will the writer, losing capital, start to indulge new child?

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its initial letter, which is lost
the start of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: Will Self is an English novelist
first letter
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A will-maker wonders whether to spoil the latest baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like a testament, but it is the first name of the novelist Will Self.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides the adjective, elfin is a noun for a little elf, and so a small child; the question mark flags that rare sense.

clue.text: Windows, for example around Departments, displaying price

indicators.note: 'around' wraps the first piece about the second

blocks.note: Windows is an operating system, OS
D is the abbreviation for department, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Shop windows in a department store show the price tags.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookmaker's odds are the price offered on a bet, as in 'a starting price of ten to one'.

clue.text: Sit on swings during publicity stunt Director knocked out

indicators.note: something that swings moves to and fro, so the letters are moved about
'during' places the jumbled pair inside the word for a stunt

blocks.note: taken as written
hype is exaggerated promotion
D is the abbreviation for director

explanation.surface: A film director is floored when a promotional stunt involves sitting on playground swings.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hypnotised is put into a trance, dazed and senseless as if knocked out.
